entities.summary:
Joseph-François-Louis-Charles de Damas (1758–1829), Duke of Damas, was a prominent French general and staunch royalist whose career spanned the tumultuous transition from the Ancien Régime through the French Revolution and Empire to the Bourbon Restoration. Born into the high nobility on October 28, 1758, in Paris, his life was inextricably linked with the fate of the Bourbon monarchy. He distinguished himself early as a cavalry officer, serving as aide-de-camp to his uncle, the Marquis de Damas, and later as a colonel in the Royal-Dauphin Cavalry, embodying the military elite loyal to Louis XVI prior to 1789.

Upon the outbreak of the French Revolution, Damas remained steadfastly loyal to the crown, participating in the ill-fated Flight to Varennes in June 1791 as a trusted aide. Following the royal family's capture, he emigrated, joining the Armée des Princes, the émigré army formed in Coblence under the command of the Prince de Condé. Here, he actively participated in campaigns against revolutionary France from 1792 to 1797, serving as a maréchal de camp and playing a direct role in the efforts to restore the monarchy by force. His military service continued in various royalist capacities across Europe during the Napoleonic era, including a period in the service of Russia, awaiting the opportune moment for the Bourbons' return.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Joseph-François-Louis-Charles de Damas represents a significant figure within the French aristocracy whose unwavering loyalty shaped the counter-revolutionary movements and the subsequent Bourbon Restoration. His career provides crucial insight into the military and political dynamics of royalist émigrés and the challenges of re-establishing monarchical rule in post-revolutionary France.
